prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, whose magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms opened a new regime of frequency-standard accuracy

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are the one candidate on this shortlist where the discovery is a single, sharply defined idea with a decisive realisation: trap many atoms at the magic wavelength so that the light shift cancels, then interrogate them in parallel. The result is fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, which changed what can be measured, from relativistic geodesy to bounds on drifting constants and the coming redefinition of the second. It has been independently reproduced with strontium, ytterbium and other species in laboratories on several continents, and international clock comparisons are now routine, so the maturity question is settled. Katori supplied the magic-wavelength proposal and first lattice-clock realisation; Ye's group carried the clock to record accuracy and into the many-body regime. Two laureates is a coherent, fair split. Broad support in the openings (five top-three placements, two first places, seven members ranking it) is not my argument, but it does tell me the physics case is not idiosyncratic to atomic physicists.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the subject sits close to prizes already given: the 2005 prize for the frequency comb and the 2012 prize for ion control, which included Wineland's optical ion clocks. If one reads the field as a single precision-measurement programme, a third prize looks redundant. There is also an attribution gap: other strontium and ytterbium groups (including the Paris and PTB efforts) and ultrastable-laser developers made decisive contributions that two names cannot represent, and the practical payoff through a redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so some of the impact is still prospective.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B005 third and flags that the 2005 comb prize and 2012 ion-control prize partly overlap in subject, which could reduce the committee's appetite for another precision-measurement award.
responses.response: I take the overlap seriously but think it is about subject area, not the achievement. The comb is the gearbox that counts optical cycles and the ion clock is a different atomic system with a different limiting uncertainty. The lattice clock rests on a separate conceptual step, the magic wavelength, which allows a very large number of atoms to be interrogated at once and so changes the statistical and systematic budget. The two earlier prizes are precisely what made a 1e-18 lattice clock readable and usable, so I regard them as context rather than prior recognition. Where I agree with Mehlig is that the citation must state the invention narrowly, which is why mine names the lattice and magic-wavelength trapping explicitly.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B005 first from a laser-spectroscopy standpoint and asks whether the committee would prefer to group lattice clocks with ultrastable-laser or frequency-comb work, which would change the allocation.
responses.response: I agree with the ranking and with the measurement-limited argument, but I would resist grouping. Folding ultrastable lasers into the citation would add names and dilute a clean invention-plus-realisation story that fits two people. I also qualify one point: Kroll's framing treats the laser as nearly part of the clock, whereas in the attribution I would keep the atomic idea, trapping and probing at the magic wavelength, as the thing being rewarded and leave the laser stabilisation as enabling technology. That choice is open to challenge, since the cavity and laser work arguably set the stability that Ye's group exploited.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first and argues that it is original, mature and not duplicated by the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in circuits, while noting that Wallraff is missing from the credited trio and that he may be biased towards a field he works in.
responses.response: I respect the candour about bias and agree that B046 is scientifically excellent. My doubt is about the proximity to 2025, where the same superconducting platform was honoured only a year ago, and about attribution: the first strong-coupling experiment belongs to Wallraff, who is outside the credited names, and Devoret and Nakamura also made decisive early demonstrations. A prize that omits the experimental demonstrator is harder to defend than the lattice-clock pair, where the invention and the best realisation map onto two people. I would put B046 below B005 for those reasons, not because of any lack of impact.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the IceCube discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos first, as a foundational observational result that opened neutrino astronomy, while accepting that any trio omits many collaboration members and early pioneers.
responses.response: The scientific case is strong, and I agree that detection of the diffuse flux is stable. My hesitation is that this is a collaboration-scale discovery, and Pearce's own attribution paragraph shows how arbitrary a three-person choice would be given AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND. Source identification is also still partial, so the prize would rest on the flux rather than on a settled source picture. I would keep B035 as a serious candidate for a later year, but for now I think the lattice-clock allocation is cleaner and the discovery more fully matured.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first, calling the theory prediction followed by experimental discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity clean and timely, and ranks B005 only sixth because the SI redefinition is pending.
responses.response: I agree with the strength of B014 and I put it second. On timing I disagree about B005: waiting for the SI redefinition makes a prize depend on a metrological committee's schedule, whereas the scientific discovery, accuracy near 1e-18 reproduced in many laboratories, is already complete. By contrast the superconducting mechanism in magic-angle graphene is unresolved, and Eriksson's own uncertainty about earlier theory credit (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto) bears on the three-name allocation. I would not call B014 premature, but its attribution is less settled than B005's.

uncertainties: Whether the committee would accept a third precision-measurement award after the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
Whether early lattice-clock work by other groups, or ultrastable-laser developers, has a claim strong enough to make a two-person credit look incomplete.
How much weight the pending redefinition of the second should carry in timing the award.
Whether I am overweighting a precision-atomic-physics argument that a committee member from another field would weigh differently.
statement.conflict_note: My profile documents no personal tie to either Katori or Ye. The documented connections are to Anne L'Huillier and the Lund attosecond group, Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich, Ingvar Lindgren's Gothenburg group, and Schuch, Dahlstrom, Argenti and Indelicato; none of these is a credited name for B005. I am a theoretical atomic physicist working in an adjacent area, which I flag as a possible bias towards the field, but no specific conflict or recusal issue is apparent from the provided profile.
